title: Tenant entropy, stability, and runtime safeguards
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook defines pragmatic safeguards, operational controls, and runbook procedures to manage tenant-level entropy (unpredictable resource usage, thermal events, KV cache churn, and noisy neighbors) in private VPC and on-prem Redwood deployments. The goal is to preserve tenant SLAs while providing clear escalation, telemetry, and rollback actions for field operators.

Scope: applies to Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments running the Redwood runtime (all supported versions) and to operator teams responsible for tenant onboarding, capacity zoning, and steady-state ops.

Audience: SRE/Field Ops, Private Deploy Customer Engineers, Platform Reliability, and Solutions Engineering.

Key concepts and definitions

- Tenant entropy: any sudden or non-linear divergence in a tenant's resource or behavioral profile (examples: bursty seq-length distributions, KV cache thrash, high-attention memory growth due to long-context requests).
- Containment: automated or manual actions that limit blast radius (rate limiting, synthetic throttles, eviction, tenant quarantine).
- Soft vs hard fallback: soft falls redirect to compatible model variants or reduced batch sizes; hard falls stop new sessions to protect cluster core functions.

SLOs and operational thresholds

- Per-tenant P99 latency SLO for interactive endpoints: 95% of tenants remain below 750ms P99 under normal load.
- System-wide total GPU utilization target: 55-85% steady state; sustained >90% triggers containment flow.
- KV cache hit rate guardrail: for production tenants, maintain >65% prefix hit rate; a sustained drop >20ppts for >10 minutes should trigger investigation.
- Thermal margin: GPU temperature > 78C sustained for 2 minutes -> schedule immediate workload shedding on affected host.

Telemetry and alerting (minimum required)

- Alerts and dashboards must include: per-tenant latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), per-tenant token/sec, per-host GPU temp, KV cache hit rate, batch size distribution, and evictions/sec.
- Anomaly detection: baseline models should compute expected token/sec and seq-length histogram; deviations >3 std dev for 5 minutes generate an incident candidate.

Containment controls (catalog)

1) Tenant soft-throttle (recommended first line)
   - API-layer token-per-second cap that reduces new requests without dropping active sessions.
   - Typical config: 75% of historical 95th percentile traffic for 10m, then reassess.

2) Adaptive batching limit
   - Temporarily reduce max_batch_tokens and max_batch_size per tenant to preserve tail latency.
   - CLI example: redwoodctl tenant update --id T-123 --set "max_batch_tokens=1024,max_batch_size=8"

3) Model variant fallback
   - Route new requests to a lower-memory variant or lower-precision quantized model. This is considered a soft fallback if output quality degradation is acceptable per customer policy.

4) Quarantine mode (hard containment)
   - Throttle to 0 new sessions, allow graceful shutdown of in-flight requests, and retain data for postmortem. Use only when tenant causes instability across multiple hosts.

Operational runbook: containment flow (step-by-step)

1) Detection (automatic or manual)
   - Alert fires (eg. tenant-p99-degrade or kv-cache-drop) -> Pager duty to on-call SRE.

2) Rapid triage (5–10 minutes)
   - Identify tenant and affected hosts: run: redwoodctl observe tenant --id T-123 --range 15m
   - Check host-level signals: GPU temps, host load, eviction counts.
   - If only single-host and thermal/host metrics are abnormal -> proceed to host isolation (step 3a).

3) Containment actions (choose path)
   - 3a) Host isolation and workload drain:
       * Mark host unschedulable: redwoodctl host cordon HOST-45
       * Drain running tasks with graceful window: redwoodctl host drain HOST-45 --grace 120s
       * Monitor latency impact for 3 minutes.
   - 3b) Tenant soft-throttle and batch limit (if cross-host):
       * Apply tenant soft-throttle: redwoodctl tenant throttle --id T-123 --rps 0.75x-historical-95th
       * Reduce batching: redwoodctl tenant update --id T-123 --set "max_batch_tokens=512,max_batch_size=4"
   - 3c) Model fallback (if throughput still exceeds capacity):
       * Update routing policy to fallback model variant: redwoodctl route update --tenant T-123 --fallback-model model-x-q4_0
   - 3d) Quarantine (last resort):
       * Enable quarantine mode: redwoodctl tenant quarantine --id T-123 --reason "stability-incident" --retain-logs true

4) Stabilization and monitoring (10–60 minutes)
   - Confirm P99 and KV hit rate return to baseline. Maintain containment controls for minimum 30m after stabilization unless rollback is required.

5) Post-incident actions
   - Create incident ticket and attach: tenant traffic traces (last 2 hours), host thermal logs, and KV eviction timeline.
   - Run targeted replay tests in staging with the tenant's traffic profile to reproduce.
   - If containment involved model fallback, schedule a quality check with Customer Success.

Rollback and upgrade safety guidance (partial upgrades, stateful components)

- Principle: always prefer conservative, customer-safe rollouts when runtime state (KV caches, tenant-to-host mappings) is involved.
- Pre-upgrade checklist (operator-run):
  1) Snapshot KV cache: redwoodctl kv snapshot --tenant T-123 --out /snapshots/T-123-$(date +%F).tar.gz
  2) Verify snapshot integrity; store to customer-designated storage if required by contract.
  3) Enable canary sizing: apply upgrade to 2–5% of hosts that service <3 production tenants, observe for 30–60 minutes.
  4) If canary shows >10% increase in P99 or sustained KV hit-rate drop >15ppts, abort rollout.

- Rollback procedure (stateful rollback):
  1) Freeze routing to upgraded hosts: redwoodctl route freeze --version vX.Y
  2) Restore KV snapshot if corruption suspected: redwoodctl kv restore --from /snapshots/T-123-2026-02-01.tar.gz --tenant T-123
  3) Revert model runtime binary to previous artifact and redeploy host: redwoodctl host deploy --host HOST-45 --artifact redwood-runtime:vX.Y-1
  4) Reintroduce traffic only after health checks pass for 3 consecutive 1-minute windows.

Day-2 housekeeping and preventative controls

- Run daily synthetic probes per tenant that sample seq-length distributions and measure prefix hit-rate regression. Maintain a rolling 7-day baseline.
- Weekly: thermal calibration sweep; sample idle power and GPU temperature drift across zones.
- Monthly: tenant-level cost and entropic-risk review (top 5 tenants by variance).

Operator playbook for workload shaping (templates)

- Rapid soft-throttle template:
  redwoodctl tenant throttle --id <TENANT_ID> --rps <value> --duration 30m --note "auto containment due to P99 spike"

- Model fallback template:
  redwoodctl route update --tenant <TENANT_ID> --fallback-model <MODEL_ID> --priority 90 --duration 1h

Configuration reference (table)

| Setting | Recommended default | Rationale | When to change |
|---------|---------------------|-----------|----------------|
| max_batch_tokens | 2048 | Balances latency and throughput for medium-length contexts | High-latency customer interactive workloads |
| max_batch_size | 16 | Limits memory pressure at peak | Small-GPU or high-variance tenants |
| kv_cache_eviction_threshold | 80% | Prevents sustained swap and OOM | If eviction spike observed >200/s |
| tenant_soft_throttle_window | 10m | Short window for automated containment | Longer if oscillation persists |

Operational ownership and contacts

- Primary owner: Private Deployments SRE (on-call rotation). Contact: oncall-private@redwood.ai
- Secondary: Field Ops (Customer Engineering). Pager: +1-415-555-0189 (escalation).
- Product contact for model fallback policies: Mei Lin (mei.lin@redwood.ai).

Example diagnostic snippets

- Inspecting tenant traffic histogram (last 30m):
  redwoodctl observe tenant --id T-123 --metrics seq_length_histogram,token_rate --range 30m --output json

- KV cache hit rate quick check (per host):
  ssh operator@host-45 'sudo redwood-runtime-admin metric get kv_hit_rate --last 10m'

FAQs and decision guidance

- Q: When do we prefer model fallback vs throttle?
  A: Prefer model fallback when latency is budgeted but memory/thermal limits are the cause. Prefer throttle when the tenant's absolute token/sec threatens cluster-wide stability.

- Q: Can quarantine be automated?
  A: Quarantine automation is supported but must be enabled per-customer in the onboarding contract. By default quarantine is manual to avoid customer surprise.

Appendix: fields and evidence to attach to incident tickets

- Tenant trace ID list (CSV), per-host GPU thermal logs, KV snapshots (if taken), routing policy at time-of-incident, and a summary of containment actions taken with timestamps.
